advaita.english: Know prakṛti (matter-nature) and puruṣa (the conscious principle) as the two prakṛti of Īśvara (the Lord), both anādi (without beginning): since the Lord is eternal, His two natures must be eternal too, and to possess these two is precisely what makes Him Lord. Those who split anādī as 'not the first' so as to keep the Lord as sole cause are wrong, for before the two arose there would be nothing to rule, and saṃsāra (the round of birth), bondage and release would become causeless and scripture pointless. Know the vikāra (modifications), from buddhi (intellect) down to body and senses, and the guṇa (qualities) that turn into pleasure, pain and delusion, as born of prakṛti, which is the Lord's triguṇa māyā (three-stranded power of manifestation).
advaita.divergence_note: Śaṅkara (source 13.20) makes the pair the Lord's two powers rather than two independent reals, and spends his argument refuting a rival tatpuruṣa parsing (na ādī) of anādī; prakṛti is explicitly identified with triguṇa māyā. Guṇa are read as the pleasure-pain-delusion forms of cognition, not as ethical virtues (contrast Rāmānuja).

viśiṣṭādvaita.english: Know that prakṛti (matter) and puruṣa (the self), mutually conjoined, are both anādi (beginningless). And know that both the vikāra (modifications) such as desire and aversion, which cause bondage, and the guṇa (qualities) such as amānitva (freedom from pride) and the rest, which cause release, are born of prakṛti. This same prakṛti, joined to the self from time without beginning and transformed into the form of the kṣetra (field, the body), binds the self through desire and aversion, and that very prakṛti, through humility and the other virtues, becomes the cause of its apavarga (liberation).
viśiṣṭādvaita.divergence_note: Rāmānuja (source 13.19) reads vikāra as the passions (icchā-dveṣa) and, strikingly, guṇa as the virtues listed at 13.7-11 (amānitva etc.), so the half-verse becomes a statement that one and the same prakṛti supplies both the chains and the means of release. No school but Vallabha (who follows him) takes guṇa this way; for Śaṅkara, Śrīdhara and Madhusūdana guṇa are the pleasure-pain-delusion modes.

dvaita.english: To explain 'from what, what arises' (13.4), the Lord sums up prakṛti (matter), its vikāra (products) and puruṣa (the conscious being). The guṇa are sattva (clarity) and the rest; the vikāra are named separately because they are only a very slight particularization of the guṇa, arising as creation out of dissolution, as the Mādhucchandasa recension says.
dvaita.divergence_note: THIN: Madhva's supplied comment (source 13.20) is three sentences and does not gloss anādi or say who the puruṣa is here; it only frames the verse as answering 13.4 and explains why vikāra are listed apart from guṇa (slight difference, laya to sarga), citing a Mādhucchandasa text. Rendering kept to what is there; no Dvaita reading of the jīva-Īśvara relation is supplied for this verse.

śuddhādvaita.english: This is the Bhagavat's own sāṅkhya (enumeration of principles), not that of the sāṅkhya partisans for whom prakṛti is an eternal second beside the self: here prakṛti is the Lord's śakti (power), in two forms, as effect the upādhi (limiting adjunct) of the jīva (individual self) bound with avidyā (ignorance), and as cause the māyā of the paramātman (supreme self); likewise puruṣa is the aṃśin (whole), the root person, and the jīva are His aṃśa (portions). By līlā (play), by His own will, He took up prakṛti; know both as My aṃśa, sat-cit (being-consciousness) in nature, anādi because not other than their cause. Know the vikāra, desire and aversion that bind, and the guṇa, humility and the rest, or sattva and the rest, that lead to amṛta (immortality), as born of prakṛti.
śuddhādvaita.divergence_note: Vallabha (source 13.20) repositions the whole verse inside a 'Bhagavadīya sāṅkhya' and doubles each term: prakṛti as effect (jīva's adjunct) and as cause (the Lord's māyā), puruṣa as root-whole and as portions. Beginninglessness comes from non-difference from the cause, not from independent eternity, and the taking-up of prakṛti is līlā (Bhāgavata 3.26.4-5). He keeps Rāmānuja's virtue-reading of guṇa but offers sattva etc. as an alternative.

bhakti.english: With this verse and the next four the Lord expounds 'what its modifications are and from what it comes, who he is and what his power', by declaring prakṛti and puruṣa the causes of saṃsāra (the round of birth). Know both as anādi (beginningless), for if they had a beginning, another prakṛti would be needed for them, and so without end; prakṛti is beginningless as the śakti (power) of the beginningless Īśvara, and puruṣa is beginningless as His aṃśa (portion), a point Śaṅkara has argued at length, so I do not expand it. Know the vikāra, body, senses and the rest, and the guṇa, their transformations as pleasure, pain and delusion, as sprung from prakṛti.
bhakti.divergence_note: Śrīdhara (source 13.20) gives a regress (anavasthā) argument for beginninglessness and grounds it devotionally: prakṛti as the Lord's power, puruṣa as His portion. He explicitly defers to Śaṅkara's bhāṣya for the full proof, so his divergence from Advaita here is in the aṃśa language, not in a rival argument.

advaita-bhakti.english: In the seventh chapter the Lord set out His two prakṛti, the lower, which is the kṣetra (field), and the higher, which is the jīva (living being); here the lower is called prakṛti, the three-stranded māyā, the power of the Supreme Lord, and the higher is called puruṣa, so there is no contradiction. Know both as anādi (without a cause): prakṛti because it is the cause of the whole world and to seek a cause for it would be endless regress; puruṣa because the joy, grief and fear of every newborn are driven by its past dharma and adharma (merit and demerit), else one would suffer the unearned and lose the earned. Know the vikāra, the sixteen (five great elements and eleven senses), and the guṇa, sattva, rajas and tamas as pleasure, pain and delusion, as having prakṛti alone for their cause.
advaita-bhakti.divergence_note: Madhusūdana (source 13.20) harmonizes the verse with 7.4-6 (aparā and parā prakṛti) and gives two separate proofs of beginninglessness: regress for prakṛti, the karmic argument (kṛtahāni-akṛtābhyāgama) for puruṣa. His vikāra are the classical sixteen, a narrower count than Śaṅkara's 'buddhi down to body and senses'.

so_what_questions: If the raw material of my temperament had no starting point, am I responsible for it or only for what I do with it?
Are my worst reactions and my best habits made of the same stuff, and if so, does that change how I work on them?
When I say 'I am anxious' or 'I am confident', which part of me is actually doing the feeling?
Is it possible to stop asking 'when did this pattern start?' and still change it?
If my body, moods and abilities are all products of one underlying nature, what is left that I can call me?
Should I treat my team's personalities as fixed givens, or as material that can be reshaped?

everyday_applications.advaita: When you catch yourself saying 'I am a stressed person', notice that the stress, the body and even the clever mind analysing it are all listed here as products of one power, none of them the knower. A manager can stop trying to fix a team's moods by argument and start by refusing to treat any mood, including their own, as who they are.
everyday_applications.viśiṣṭādvaita: The same material that produces your envy at a colleague's promotion can produce your humility; Rāmānuja says one nature makes both. So the practical work is not escaping your nature but redirecting it: the energy of a resentful afternoon can be turned, deliberately, into the patience and modesty that actually free you.
everyday_applications.dvaita: Madhva's note is a reminder to keep categories clean: the basic qualities of a situation and the specific products they turn into are almost the same, but not identical, and worth naming separately. A doctor separating a patient's general constitution from the particular symptom it has produced is doing exactly this.
everyday_applications.śuddhādvaita: Vallabha would have a parent see both the child and the messy circumstances of the child's life as portions of the same source, taken up in play rather than as a punishment. That reframes a chaotic household not as a problem to be solved before joy is allowed, but as the field where the play is already happening.
everyday_applications.bhakti: Śrīdhara's regress argument is useful when you get stuck asking 'but what caused that?' about a family conflict or an organisational mess: at some point the chain has no first link, and the only useful question is how you act now. He then leaves the long proofs to someone else, a good model for a teacher who knows when to point to the textbook.
everyday_applications.advaita-bhakti: Madhusūdana's karmic argument says a newborn's fear and joy are not random; they carry history. A founder inheriting a company's culture can use this: the reactions people bring on day one have causes older than you, so diagnose before you blame, and do not expect a new policy to erase what came before it.

self_assessment: All six bhāṣya read in full. Strongest divergence is on guṇa: Rāmānuja and Vallabha read them as liberating virtues (amānitva etc.) opposite binding passions, while Śaṅkara, Śrīdhara and Madhusūdana read them as pleasure-pain-delusion modes. Anādi is grounded differently in each: the Lord's eternity (Śaṅkara), non-difference from cause (Vallabha), regress (Śrīdhara), regress plus karma (Madhusūdana). Madhva's supplied text is thin and flagged.
